clue.text: Lawyer to cover up material

blocks.note: DA is a District Attorney, an American public prosecutor
to mask something is to hide or cover it up

explanation.surface: A lawyer hides some damning document or evidence from view.
explanation.definitionFit: Damask is a patterned woven fabric, typically silk or linen, used for tablecloths and furnishings.

clue.text: It’s bent to sell drugs

definitions.note: read as 'it is a bent thing', naming the noun

blocks.note: a shop that does sandwiches sells them
gear is slang for illegal drugs

explanation.surface: A corrupt figure is set on dealing narcotics.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bent' is British slang for corrupt, which is the surface's trap; here it means folded.
explanation.definitionFit: A dog-ear is the corner of a page that has been folded down, so it is something bent.

clue.text: German city cut one friend of the town

indicators.note: cutting something shortens it, so the final letter is lopped off

blocks.note: Munich is the Bavarian capital
I is the Roman numeral for one
a pal is a friend

explanation.surface: A German city drops one of its twin-town friendships.
explanation.definitionFit: Municipal means relating to a town or its local government, as in a municipal library.

clue.text: Talk at length about an uncritical friend

indicators.note: about means around, so the first word goes round the next

blocks.note: a spiel is a long, glib speech
taken as written

explanation.surface: Holding forth endlessly about a pal who never finds fault.
explanation.walkthrough: 'friend' suggests a person; the uncritical friend here is a dog, loyal whatever its owner does.
explanation.definitionFit: A spaniel is a famously devoted dog, the image of a companion that adores its owner without judgement.

clue.text: Lively one I paired off

blocks.note: an is the indefinite article, meaning one
taken as written
animals that have mated have been paired off

explanation.surface: Someone cheerful talks about having been coupled up with a partner.
explanation.definitionFit: Animated describes a person full of energy and spirit, a close synonym in ordinary usage.

clue.text: Deal she sent Noel despite everything

indicators.note: dealing cards follows shuffling them, so these letters come out in a new order

blocks.note: the letters taken as written

explanation.surface: She kept an arrangement with Noel in place whatever happened.
explanation.definitionFit: Nonetheless means in spite of that, so it is an adverb for carrying on regardless.

clue.text: Weakling makes the most of work

blocks.note: to milk a situation is to exploit it fully
OP is short for opus, a musical work

explanation.surface: A feeble person exploits every bit of the job going.
explanation.definitionFit: A milksop is a timid, ineffectual man, an old insult for someone lacking courage.

clue.text: Perfect maybe, given top scores by judge finally

indicators.note: finally points to the closing letter of the word before it

blocks.note: ten is the top mark a judge can give
the closing letter of judge

explanation.surface: A flawless routine earns maximum marks from the judges.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Perfect' looks like praise but is a grammar term; 'maybe' signals an example.
explanation.definitionFit: The perfect is a grammatical tense, as in 'I have eaten', so it is one example of the category.

clue.text: Maniac called, caught in the act

definitions.note: a noun defining an adjective, read as 'like a maniac'

indicators.note: caught in means held inside, so one word sits within the other

blocks.note: to ring someone is to call them on the phone
a deed is an act

explanation.surface: A madman phoned and was caught red-handed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'caught in the act' reads as one idiom, but 'caught in' is the instruction and 'the act' is the outer word.
explanation.definitionFit: Deranged means insane, the state of a maniac, though the clue gives the noun for the adjective.

clue.text: Government to neuter armed criminal

blocks.note: G is a standard abbreviation for government
to unman is to castrate, or to deprive of manly qualities

explanation.surface: The state sets out to disarm a dangerous offender.
explanation.definitionFit: A gunman is a criminal carrying a firearm, so the phrase is a plain description of one.

clue.text: Using the internet encompasses ‘electronic’ right? – it’s not much of a joke

definitions.text: it’s not much of a joke

indicators.note: to encompass is to surround, so the first word wraps round what follows

blocks.note: someone using the internet is online
E is the usual abbreviation for electronic, as in e-mail
R is the standard abbreviation for right

explanation.surface: A joke about web life gets a dismissive verdict: hardly a joke at all.
explanation.definitionFit: A one-liner is a gag told in a single sentence, so it is literally not much of a joke in length.

clue.text: One making designs for the Arctic melting

indicators.note: something melting loses its shape and runs into a new form, so these letters are rearranged

blocks.note: the letters taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone drawing up plans with the polar ice cap's thaw in mind.
explanation.definitionFit: An architect draws up the plans for buildings, so designing is the core of the job.

clue.text: Implements taken to table resignation out of order

indicators.note: something out of order is not in its proper sequence, so the letters get rearranged

blocks.note: the letters taken as written

explanation.surface: Tools are brought to a meeting to put forward a resignation improperly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'table' suggests tabling a motion; here it is the dinner table.
explanation.definitionFit: Eating irons is a jocular name for cutlery, the knives and forks brought to the dinner table.

clue.text: Back lacking flexibility

blocks.note: first meaning: the rear part of a ship
second meaning: strict, severe, unyielding

explanation.surface: Someone with a rigid spine and no suppleness.
explanation.definitionFit: Stern is the rear of a vessel, and as an adjective describes a severe, unbending manner.

clue.text: Award for newsmen – withdraw it, not expected to be broadcast

indicators.note: something broadcast is heard on air, so the words are judged by their sound

blocks.note: to pull something is to withdraw it
a surprise is something not expected

explanation.surface: A newspaper award is to be scrapped, an unforeseen announcement on air.
explanation.walkthrough: Said quickly, 'pull it, surprise' runs into the name of the prize.
explanation.definitionFit: The Pulitzer Prizes are the leading American awards for journalism, given to reporters and editors.

clue.text: Unsupported belief in education

blocks.note: taken as written
tuition is teaching or instruction

explanation.surface: A conviction held without evidence about how schooling works.
explanation.definitionFit: An intuition is a feeling or belief reached without conscious reasoning or proof.

clue.text: Operator takes time as producer of caviar

indicators.note: to take something in is to hold it, so one word goes inside the other

blocks.note: a surgeon operates on patients
T is the abbreviation for time

explanation.surface: A worker takes time out to become a supplier of fish eggs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Operator' suggests a machine or phone operator; a surgeon is the one who operates.
explanation.definitionFit: Caviar is the salted roe of the sturgeon, so the fish is literally its producer.

clue.text: Hot gospeller having tangle with evilest deviant

indicators.note: deviant means straying from the norm, so the letters stray from their order

blocks.note: taken as written
joins the two words of fodder
taken as written

explanation.surface: A fiery preacher squares up to the worst of sinners.
explanation.definitionFit: A hot gospeller is a zealous evangelical preacher; a televangelist does that preaching on television.

clue.text: Football team to harvest criminal

blocks.note: Aston Villa is a Birmingham football club, known as Villa
to in is an old verb for gathering in a crop

explanation.surface: A football club out to reap the rewards of crime.
explanation.definitionFit: A villain is a wrongdoer, and in British slang specifically a criminal.

clue.text: Slim men seldom topped and tailed giant

indicators.note: with head and foot trimmed away, only the inside of the phrase is left

blocks.note: found running through the middle of this phrase, with its outer letters dropped

explanation.surface: Thin men are rarely huge, a contrast drawn about body sizes.
explanation.walkthrough: Strip SL from the front and LDOM from the back of the run of letters to leave the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Giant as an adjective means enormous, so it is a direct synonym for vast in size.

clue.text: Cover loose rock facing north

blocks.note: scree is a mass of loose stones on a mountainside
N is the abbreviation for north

explanation.surface: Taking shelter behind a slope of loose stones that looks north.
explanation.definitionFit: A screen hides or shelters something, and to screen is to cover it from view.

clue.text: Rise and dance round front of ballroom

indicators.note: the front of a word is its opening letter, so only that is kept
round means going about the outside, so one piece encloses the other

blocks.note: a reel is a lively Scottish dance
the opening letter of ballroom

explanation.surface: Getting up to take a turn on the ballroom floor.
explanation.definitionFit: To rise up, as in an uprising, is to rebel against authority; both are verbs.

clue.text: Wish luck to British minor

blocks.note: B is the abbreviation for British
less means smaller or lesser in importance

explanation.surface: Sending good wishes to a young British person.
explanation.definitionFit: To bless someone is to call down divine favour on them, a way of wishing them good fortune.

clue.text: Settled? No I’m tossing in bed endlessly

definitions.text: Settled? No I’m tossing in bed endlessly

blocks.clueFragment: Settled? No I’m tossing in bed endlessly
blocks.note: surface reading: someone asked if they are comfortable says they keep turning over all night
setter's reading: the speaker is a person who habitually cannot sleep

explanation.surface: Asked whether they have settled down, a restless sleeper complains of endless turning.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is the reply of a chronic poor sleeper; no wordplay was found to build the letters, so it is read as a cryptic definition.
explanation.definitionFit: An insomniac is a person who regularly cannot get to sleep, and so lies restless through the night.

clue.text: Twist a lever to lift

indicators.note: to twist is to wrench out of shape, so the letters are put in a new order

blocks.note: the letters taken as written
taken as written, part of the fodder

explanation.surface: An instruction to pull a lever so that something rises.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to' looks like a link before 'lift' but its letters belong to the anagram.
explanation.definitionFit: Elevator is the American word for what the British call a lift, the cage that carries people between floors.

clue.text: Member of government party imprisoned

blocks.note: the party in office are 'the ins', so one of them is in
a side is a party or faction in a dispute

explanation.surface: A minister from the ruling party has been locked up.
explanation.walkthrough: Inside is informal for in prison, as in 'doing time inside'.
explanation.definitionFit: Being inside is everyday slang for serving a prison sentence, so it means locked up in jail.

clue.text: What did for cat functions when child comes back round

indicators.note: coming back means returning the way one came, so the word is read from right to left
round means surrounding, so the turned word goes about the other

blocks.note: a son is a child
sines are trigonometric functions

explanation.surface: Something ended a cat's life after a child returned home.
explanation.walkthrough: The proverb is 'curiosity killed the cat', and nosiness is a kind of curiosity.
explanation.definitionFit: Nosiness is prying inquisitiveness, and the proverb says that trait is what killed the cat.

clue.text: American pioneer working as standard

blocks.note: William Penn founded the colony of Pennsylvania
a machine that is working is on

explanation.surface: A founding settler of America serves as a model for others.
explanation.definitionFit: A pennon is a long narrow flag, and a standard is a flag or banner carried as an emblem.
